frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve leverage with Europe. Price volatility and European diversification efforts could gradually reduce that influence.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya pressures Algeria’s borders and complicates its non-interventionist security doctrine. Foreign military and intelligence activity in the region remains a sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: China remains central to Angola’s infrastructure, trade, and oil-backed financing ecosystem, limiting Luanda’s room for maneuver despite debt-management efforts. Refinancing and commodity-price shocks remain key vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor attracts U.S., European, and Gulf interest as an alternative route for critical minerals from the Copperbelt. Competition over logistics, mineral access, and regulatory control could test Angola’s bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou is strengthening its role as a gateway for the Sahel, but trade restrictions and political tensions with neighboring states can disrupt transit revenues. Foreign investment in port and logistics infrastructure also creates long-term influence concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Jihadist Encroachment
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and militant activity near the northern borders with Burkina Faso and Niger are increasing pressure on Benin’s security budget and transport corridors. External security assistance is expanding, but dependence could narrow strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains significant influence over diamond governance through its partnership with De Beers, but the relationship remains central to national revenue and marketing access. Lab-grown diamonds and weaker global demand threaten future leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in Botswana’s copper, nickel, and other minerals is rising as foreign firms seek diversified supply chains. The government must balance investment attraction with local beneficiation and environmental protections.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation and control over gold production, challenging established foreign mining arrangements. Disputes over licenses, taxation, and operating security could deter investment while informal extraction expands.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burkina Faso’s turn away from French support toward Russian-linked security assistance has increased geopolitical dependence without resolving the insurgency. Attacks continue to threaten mines, roads, and national control over resource zones.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Bujumbura is seeking tighter control over nickel, gold, and rare-mineral operations, but weak institutions and opaque licensing limit effective sovereign capture of revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed groups and border accusations, raising risks for trade corridors and external security dependence.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and maritime-security development relies heavily on European, American, and multilateral financing, giving partners substantial strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains vulnerable to trans-Atlantic drug trafficking and illegal fishing, requiring sustained foreign intelligence, patrol, and judicial support.

highlights: Oil and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector capture
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and mining revenues remain constrained by opaque contracting, elite brokerage, and foreign commercial interests, limiting broad domestic gains.

frictionVectors.title: Separatist conflict and corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone insurgency continues to disrupt production and transport in the northwest and southwest, while Chinese-backed infrastructure increases both connectivity and debt exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-resource nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain major influence over regime protection and access to gold and diamond areas, weakening transparent state control of extractive revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and porous borders with Sudan, Chad, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to obstruct roads, mining oversight, and national market integration.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain the core fiscal resource, but centralized management, opaque contracting, and infrastructure bottlenecks limit sovereign and public benefit.

frictionVectors.title: Post-French security balancing
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown of French military influence is increasing pressure on N'Djamena to diversify toward regional, Gulf, and other external partners while managing instability near Sudan and Libya.

highlights: Maritime and energy capacity slowly expanding

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte despite Comorian claims, limiting Moroni's territorial and maritime sovereignty. The dispute also drives recurring diplomatic and migration tensions.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence and weak infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Comoros remains heavily reliant on remittances, foreign aid, and imported fuel, leaving strategic infrastructure vulnerable to outside financing and supply pressure.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing foreign powers

frictionVectors.title: Conflict around eastern mineral zones
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and regional proxy dynamics continue to weaken Kinshasa's control in the east, where trade routes and mineral sites are strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign leverage over copper and cobalt
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and Gulf actors compete for access to copper, cobalt, and other critical minerals. Contractual opacity, limited domestic processing, and infrastructure-for-resources arrangements constrain value retention inside the country.

highlights: Oil remains the fiscal and geopolitical anchor

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenue and export capacity remain concentrated in oil, exposing national sovereignty to price cycles and foreign technical, financial, and trading partners.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and other projects provide essential connectivity but increase concerns over debt leverage, procurement transparency, and long-term control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire remains a major cocoa producer but captures a limited share of downstream value, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign processors, traders, and global price conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover and corridor security
frictionVectors.details: Instability in neighboring Sahel states places pressure on northern borders and transport corridors. Abidjan must balance security cooperation with preserving control over critical ports, roads, and energy links.

highlights: Port geography delivers outsized strategic leverage
Foreign bases underpin the state economy

frictionVectors.title: Competing foreign military footprints
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences generate revenue and deterrence but make Djibouti a theater for great-power rivalry and constrain independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Ethiopia corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's economy relies heavily on port activity, external financing, and Ethiopia-bound trade. Debt exposure and dependence on a single regional market limit sovereign control over infrastructure and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Gulf-linked asset pressure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs and IMF-linked reforms increase reliance on Gulf investment and asset sales, limiting Cairo's room to retain full control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains a major sovereignty and water-security dispute, with negotiations periodically stalled and unilateral operating decisions generating escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Declining hydrocarbons and foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil and gas fields leave the state dependent on foreign technical expertise and investment while production declines, weakening fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Malabo is trying to position Punta Europa as a regional gas hub, but competition from Nigeria, Cameroon and international firms constrains its bargaining power over processing and transport assets.

highlights: Red Sea position raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-controlled mining exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper and zinc projects rely heavily on external capital and expertise, leaving the state vulnerable to revenue disputes and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing regional and extra-regional security interests, increasing pressure over port access and military partnerships.

highlights: Southern Africa remains the economic lifeline
Sugar and logistics retain strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African corridors
frictionVectors.details: Trade, electricity, remittances and transport access remain closely tied to South Africa, limiting Mbabane's autonomy during regional supply or political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Diplomatic recognition pressure
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's recognition of Taiwan creates persistent pressure from China, while investment and infrastructure options remain narrower than those available to states aligned with Beijing.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD improves Ethiopia's electricity and export potential but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations and downstream guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages increase reliance on multilateral lenders and external partners, while access to ports and trade corridors remains vulnerable to regional politics.

highlights: Transition consolidates under military-led civilian rule
Oil and manganese remain strategic bargaining chips

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and mining concession opacity
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are asserting greater state control over oil, manganese, and infrastructure deals, but legacy contracts and limited transparency constrain oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependency
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors remain vulnerable to foreign commercial influence and financing conditions, particularly around mineral transport and port modernization.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential strategic partner
Cashew, fisheries, and tourism face external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and border dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional security, transport access, and energy connectivity, limiting policy autonomy despite generally cooperative relations.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak enforcement continue to threaten coastal resource control and local livelihoods.

highlights: Debt restructuring is narrowing fiscal room

frictionVectors.title: External financing and policy conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed stabilization and creditor negotiations are strengthening macroeconomic discipline while constraining spending choices and increasing sensitivity to external lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Galamsey and gold leakage
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining damages farmland and water systems while enabling informal and foreign-linked extraction networks that reduce state capture of gold value.

highlights: Junta accelerates bauxite and Simandou development

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign-led infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and mine construction is attracting major Chinese and other international capital, creating rapid export capacity but long-term dependence on externally financed corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Military rule and contract uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The junta uses resource nationalism to bolster legitimacy, yet opaque licensing, political centralization, and uncertain transition timelines weaken sovereign oversight.

highlights: Cashew exports sustain a fragile political economy

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily exposed to foreign buyers and price swings, with limited domestic processing and weak bargaining power for producers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and transshipment vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime and customs institutions leave Bissau’s port vulnerable to external commercial leverage and illicit trafficking networks, including cocaine transshipment.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF and bilateral creditors continue to shape fiscal policy, limiting Nairobi's room to subsidize energy, transport, and public services. Debt restructuring pressures remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Mombasa Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, rail, and logistics projects are increasing connectivity while raising concerns over repayment exposure, land access, and long-term control of strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but leave Lesotho dependent on cross-border infrastructure, financing, and Pretoria's purchasing power. Construction and royalty disputes remain sovereignty-sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Customs Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's manufacturing base relies heavily on external trade preferences and South African logistics. Changes in U.S. or regional market access can quickly threaten jobs and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining agreements generate export earnings and infrastructure but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and disputes over local employment and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Transport Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in ports, roads, and potential rail corridors is central to growth, yet weak state capacity limits Liberia's leverage over access fees, land use, and downstream processing.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control of production, export terminals, and budget flows. International pressure can reopen or freeze output, making sovereign resource management highly volatile.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Mercenary Influence
frictionVectors.details: External security patrons retain influence through bases, advisers, and aligned armed groups. Their presence constrains national control over infrastructure and complicates any unified energy strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects attract major foreign capital but expose Madagascar to tax disputes, environmental damage, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak transport networks increase reliance on foreign project finance and operators. Control of mining-linked roads, ports, and generation assets remains a sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-supported reforms and creditor negotiations are stabilizing the economy but limit fiscal and industrial policy space. Heavy reliance on donors leaves energy, transport, and food-security systems vulnerable to external conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Development
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, rare-earth, and uranium prospects attract foreign investors, but weak power and transport infrastructure reduce Malawi's bargaining leverage. The government faces pressure to secure better local processing and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's reliance on Russian-linked security support has increased strategic dependence while failing to eliminate insurgent threats. Western sanctions, diplomatic tension, and reduced development access constrain alternative partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Control and Informal Extraction
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to raise the state's share of gold revenues challenge foreign mining companies and may deter investment. Informal and artisanal production remains difficult to regulate and is vulnerable to armed-group taxation.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers new export revenue and regional influence, but cross-border governance, revenue expectations, and production timing create continuing friction. Mauritania remains exposed to foreign operators and global gas prices.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on iron ore exports and the long rail corridor linking mines to Nouadhibou. Foreign capital, equipment, and logistics providers retain substantial influence over this critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement and Maritime Rights
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over the Diego Garcia military facility and wider Indian Ocean security. The issue tests Port Louis's ability to convert legal recognition into effective strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Port Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius relies on imported fuel and external shipping networks, leaving it vulnerable to disruptions in Indian Ocean trade routes. Competition among India, China, Gulf investors, and Western partners creates opportunities but also strategic pressure.

highlights: Western Sahara remains the strategic fault line

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, port, and renewable-energy development in Western Sahara to reinforce its sovereignty claim. The approach continues to generate opposition from Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some international legal and commercial actors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Investment and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and American capital is expanding Morocco's ports, automotive supply chains, renewables, and defense-industrial base. Rabat retains strong negotiating capacity, but dependence on external technology and markets creates exposure to geopolitical realignment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Major gas projects rely on international operators, external finance, and foreign security support, limiting Mozambique's near-term bargaining power over revenues and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to threaten mining, logistics, and LNG assets while requiring sustained regional and international security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries are attracting international majors, creating pressure for stronger local-content rules, transparent licensing, and a larger national revenue share.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Capital Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Green-hydrogen and port projects depend heavily on European and other external capital, raising concerns over debt exposure, land access, and domestic industrial benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater control and value capture from uranium and other minerals, but technical capacity and investor confidence remain constrained.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The export route through Benin remains exposed to political rupture, border tensions, and security disruptions, limiting Niger's ability to monetize expanding oil production.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, militant attacks, and aging infrastructure continue to reduce state receipts and weaken Nigeria's control over upstream production and exports.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Operator Bargaining Power
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain important for capital and technology, while Nigeria's push for domestic refining and gas development is constrained by financing and regulatory uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Regional accusations over support to armed actors in eastern Congo continue to threaten Rwanda's access to mineral markets, aid relationships, and trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Development Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control over strategic projects but remains reliant on foreign aid, investment, and technology for energy, logistics, and mineral upgrading.

highlights: Oil Expectations Give Way to Blue Economy

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe relies on external naval partnerships and donor support to patrol its maritime zone, limiting autonomous control over offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Exploration Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Unproven offshore prospects attract foreign interest, but weak domestic capacity and disappointing exploration results constrain the country's bargaining power.

highlights: Oil and Gas Era Begins Under Fiscal Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national benefit from offshore oil and gas projects, creating friction with international operators, lenders, and prior contractual commitments.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy public debt and large infrastructure needs limit Dakar's room to pursue resource nationalism without risking financing access or investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Competition at Port Victoria
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances security and infrastructure ties with India, China, and Western partners, seeking investment without surrendering control over critical maritime assets.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Fisheries Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to foreign-owned tourism supply chains, climate shocks, and external pressure over access to fisheries and maritime resources.

highlights: Rail and Port Corridors Reshape Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining operations remain heavily dependent on foreign capital and expertise, limiting local value capture despite rising exports.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port infrastructure give overseas operators substantial influence over mineral flows, fiscal revenues, and national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Architecture
frictionVectors.details: Somalia remains dependent on foreign military, financial, and training support to secure territory and waters, weakening autonomous control over ports and offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Federal Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons attract international interest, but disputes between the federal government and member states over licensing and revenue sharing deter coherent resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral beneficiation and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Pretoria is pressing for local processing and stronger control over critical-mineral value chains while remaining dependent on foreign investment, technology, and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and logistics infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Power-sector constraints and underperforming rail and ports continue to weaken sovereign control over industrial output and expose strategic commodities to private and external logistics interests.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of oil corridors
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on external operators, financing, and Sudanese export infrastructure to monetize its oil, leaving production and revenues exposed to conflict and outside bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and armed violence sustain dependence on neighboring states, international mediation, and humanitarian systems, limiting effective control over territory and resources.

highlights: Gold and ports draw outside rivalry

frictionVectors.title: Gold-financing networks
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and paramilitary networks use gold production and export channels to finance the war, with regional and foreign buyers reducing transparent state control over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic access
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and prospective naval and logistics arrangements have become objects of external competition, while the conflict threatens the continuity of national transport and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: LNG development and contract control
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking to advance long-delayed gas exports while negotiating fiscal terms, domestic benefits, and environmental safeguards with international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, rail, and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades to Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors attract Chinese, Gulf, and other foreign capital, creating leverage over trade infrastructure even as Tanzania retains strong regulatory authority.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's expansion strengthens Togo's regional commercial leverage but leaves critical port, shipping, and logistics activity reliant on foreign operators and external trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate value-chain weakness
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources but captures limited downstream value, with financing, technology, and market access shaped by foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to migration control, limiting Tunisian policy autonomy. Domestic opposition continues to challenge the sovereignty costs of this arrangement.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gas import dependence and underperforming phosphate infrastructure weaken fiscal resilience. Delays in investment and production constrain Tunisia’s ability to convert natural resources into sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Environmental Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Uganda retains formal ownership stakes in its oil project, but financing, contractors, and export infrastructure create substantial external dependence. Environmental litigation and sanctions-related pressure continue to threaten timelines and costs.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors remain central to major transport and energy projects. Debt-service obligations could narrow Kampala’s bargaining space over strategic infrastructure and future resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: International mining companies remain dominant in extraction, smelting, and marketing despite government efforts to raise royalties and local processing. Copper price volatility leaves public finances exposed to decisions made outside Zambia.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and constrained rail corridors limit copper expansion and beneficiation. Zambia is seeking diversified investment, but Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners all compete for influence over critical logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Lithium and Mineral Deals
frictionVectors.details: Export restrictions and beneficiation demands signal stronger state control, but Chinese and other foreign investors still dominate capital, technology, and market access. Limited transparency raises concerns that increased extraction will not translate into broad domestic gains.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Currency Fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, restricted financing, and persistent currency instability weaken the state’s ability to capture and manage resource revenues. Mining companies retain significant leverage because Zimbabwe needs foreign exchange and investment.
